title: How useful is a Capital IQ-style Excel plugin for trading/research?
author: deepfit
selftext:
We’ve spent the last several weeks working on some of the less visible infrastructure behind Secmast.  We recently finished our fully integrated security master (35k tickers, 28k lineages, 25+ years), point in time, it correctly track securities and companies across ticker changes and other changes over time.

We’re also about to deploy 1-second stock and options data today, which has been a major data-engineering project on its own.

But we took a bit of a detour over the last few days and built something I’m curious about.

We created an Excel plugin that lets you pull standardized SEC financial data directly into a spreadsheet, somewhat similar to how Capital IQ works. The important part is that the numbers aren’t just dropped into Excel — you can trace them back to the underlying SEC filing/source document they came from.

For example, you could build a model in Excel using standardized income statement, balance sheet, or cash flow data and still be able to audit where each value originated.

My question for people here who actually trade or do research:

Is this useful in a trading/research workflow?

Or is this primarily something that matters to investment banking, equity research, PE, M&A, etc.?

We already have the SEC data and extraction infrastructure, so the Excel integration wasn’t a huge leap. I’m mostly trying to figure out whether it’s worth pushing further for traders or whether those are really two separate user bases.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: point in time is the part most data vendors fake. does the Excel side give the number as first reported, or the restated one when a company refiles?

replies.author: deepfit
replies.body: It’s restated to the latest filing

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: then anything backtested on it carries a look-ahead, since the restated number didn't exist on the day the trade would have fired. a flag on restated cells, or an as-first-reported toggle, would fix most of it.

replies.author: deepfit
replies.body: Our standard financials table stores both figures for each fact, value (as first filed) and value\_restated (as most recently filed), plus a restated flag.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: both columns plus a flag covers most of it. the piece a backtest still needs is the date each restated figure went public, otherwise you know the number changed but not from which bar the new one is fair to use.

replies.author: deepfit
replies.body: Awesome thanks for the input. I don’t think that would be too hard to add if we don’t already have it.
